title: BRICKSTORM Backdoor Investigation
description: Your organization has detected suspicious network activity originating from an internal host. Initial analysis suggests the presence of a backdoor malware named BRICKSTORM. Your task is to investigate the compromised host, identify the malicious activity, and contain the threat throughout its lifecycle.
outcomes: Identify and investigate suspicious services and processes.
Analyze network connections for command-and-control communications.
Contain the threat by blocking malicious communications and removing persistence mechanisms.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: Your organization has detected suspicious network activity originating from an internal host. Initial analysis suggests the presence of a backdoor malware named BRICKSTORM. This malware is known to establish persistent connections to command-and-control (C2) servers, exfiltrate data, and maintain access to compromised systems. Your task is to investigate the compromised host, identify the malicious activity, and contain the threat throughout its lifecycle. The learning objective of this scenario is to guide you through the process of identifying, analyzing, and containing a backdoor malware threat within a controlled sandbox environment. BRICKSTORM is a sophisticated malware family known for its persistence mechanisms and ability to evade detection. It typically establishes backdoor access to compromised systems, allowing attackers to maintain control and exfiltrate sensitive data.

levels.title: Initial Detection
levels.content: To prevent further malicious activity, you need to stop the suspicious process associated with the backdoor. Identify and terminate the process while minimizing impact on legitimate services. The flag you are looking for is the name of the process to terminate (a string). This task aligns with the learning objective of identifying and investigating suspicious services and processes.
levels.solution: To terminate the suspicious process, you can use the `pkill` command. For example, the command `pkill -f lab-checkin.sh` will terminate the process. The name of the process that you terminated to stop the malicious activity is `lab-checkin.sh`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Malicious processes often have unusual names or descriptions. Look for processes that do not match typical system processes.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use process management tools like `ps` or `pkill` to identify and terminate the malicious process.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The process name is `lab-checkin.sh`. Use the `pkill -f lab-checkin.sh` command to terminate it.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the host `target`. Investigate the running services on this host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services. The flag you are looking for is the name of the suspicious service (a string). This task aligns with the learning objective of identifying and investigating suspicious services and processes.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services. Look for any services that appear unusual or unauthorized. The suspicious service in this case is `updatemgr.service`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Suspicious services often have unusual names or descriptions. Look for services that do not match typical system services.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the `systemctl` command to list all running services and inspect them for any anomalies.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The suspicious service name starts with 'updatemgr'. Use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to find it.

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (IP)
levels.content: The suspicious service identified in the previous task is likely communicating with a command-and-control (C2) server. Determine the remote IP address that the service is contacting. The flag you are looking for is the IP address of the C2 server (an IPv4 address). This task aligns with the learning objective of analyzing network connections for command-and-control communications.
levels.solution: To determine the remote IP address, you can use network monitoring tools such as `netstat` or `ss` to inspect active connections. For example, the command `ss -tulnp` will show all active network connections. The IP address of the command-and-control server is `192.168.40.5`.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Command-and-control servers often communicate over unusual ports or with unexpected IP addresses. Look for connections that do not match typical network traffic.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use network monitoring tools like `ss` or `netstat` to inspect active connections and identify the destination IP address.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The C2 server IP address is `192.168.40.5`. Use the `ss -tulnp` command to confirm this.
